papers.core_contribution: Introduces a fine-grained evaluation pipeline for CoT faithfulness in LVLMs, finding that image-based biases are less articulated than text-based ones, and identifying inconsistent reasoning as a potential indicator of bias.
papers.conclusion: The study finds large variations in bias articulation rate depending on model training strategy and bias type, and identifies inconsistent reasoning as a failure mode. The 'reasonableness' of a bias affects articulation, and inconsistencies may signal biases in the absence of faithful CoTs.
papers.key_findings:
RL-trained reasoning models have substantially higher bias articulation rates compared to instruction-tuned or SFT-trained counterparts.
Visual biases are consistently less likely to be articulated than text-based biases, and subtle biases receive considerably less attention in model reasoning traces than explicit ones.
Models exhibit a previously unidentified phenomenon termed 'inconsistent reasoning' where they demonstrate correct reasoning before abruptly changing answers.
Inconsistent reasoning occurs more frequently when the bias conflicts with the ground truth, serving as a potential canary for detecting biased reasoning.
Bias articulation rates do not increase when given biased in-context samples, remaining constant across no-context, unbiased, and biased context settings.
papers.limitation:
They do not test faithfulness when inducing biases via training (as opposed to biased in-context samples).
They have yet to demonstrate detecting unfaithfulness when not explicit in the CoT in practical settings.
They do not have a theory to explain why some biases are articulated at a higher rate than others.
future_direction: Exploring faithfulness when inducing biases via training.
Demonstrating detection of unfaithfulness when not explicit in the CoT in practical settings.
Developing a theory to explain differences in bias articulation rates.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning enhances performance of large language models, but questions remain about whether these reasoning traces faithfully reflect the internal processes of the model. We present the first comprehensive study of CoT faithfulness in large vision-language models (LVLMs), investigating how both text-based and previously unexplored image-based biases affect reasoning and bias articulation. Our work introduces a novel, fine-grained evaluation pipeline for categorizing bias articulation patterns, enabling significantly more precise analysis of CoT reasoning than previous methods. This framework reveals critical distinctions in how models process and respond to different types of biases, providing new insights into LVLM CoT faithfulness. Our findings reveal that subtle image-based biases are rarely articulated compared to explicit text-based ones, even in models specialized for reasoning. Additionally, many models exhibit a previously unidentified phenomenon we term ``inconsistent'' reasoning - correctly reasoning before abruptly changing answers, serving as a potential canary for detecting biased reasoning from unfaithful CoTs. We then apply the same evaluation pipeline to revisit CoT faithfulness in LLMs across various levels of implicit cues. Our findings reveal that current language-only reasoning models continue to struggle with articulating cues that are not overtly stated.

papers.title: Output Supervision Can Obfuscate the Chain of Thought
papers.research_question: Can training against an output-only monitor (which does not see the chain of thought) still cause obfuscated chain of thought?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces and demonstrates 'feedback spillover', showing that training against an output-only monitor can obfuscate the chain of thought via parametric and conditional mechanisms, and proposes mitigations (reward targeting and Mind & Face) that achieve a Pareto improvement.
papers.conclusion: Feedback spillover is a real phenomenon that can spoil chain of thought monitorability even with output-only training; AI developers should take this risk seriously and consider implementing mitigations.
papers.key_findings:
Training against an output-only monitor can cause obfuscated chain of thought via 'feedback spillover', which occurs through parametric and conditional mechanisms.
Feedback spillover was demonstrated in three reinforcement learning environments: polynomial derivative factoring, question answering with hints, and multi-turn terminal interaction.
Two mitigations were introduced: reward targeting (to prevent conditional feedback spillover) and using separate 'Mind' and 'Face' models (to prevent parametric feedback spillover).
The mitigations, especially when combined, achieved a Pareto improvement in task performance and CoT monitorability in two environments, but destabilized training in the question-answering environment.
The work implies preserving CoT monitorability is more difficult than previously thought and offers practical recommendations for AI developers.
papers.limitation: In the question answering environment, the mitigations (especially Mind & Face) could not reduce feedback spillover without harming task performance, and applying both mitigations simultaneously destabilized training.
future_direction: Study feedback spillover in frontier models by post-training them in purpose-built environments.
Study whether existing safety post-training pipelines cause feedback spillover.
Test spillover mitigations on frontier models to yield methods with low computational and capabilities overhead.
papers.abstract: OpenAI (2025) showed that training against a chain of thought (CoT) monitor can cause obfuscated CoTs, which contain bad behavior the monitor cannot detect. They proposed to keep CoTs monitorable by training only against output monitors that do not have access to CoT. We show that such training can still cause obfuscated CoTs via two mechanisms. First, when a model is trained to produce a safe-looking output, that model may generalize to making its CoTs look safe. Second, since later tokens are conditioned on earlier ones, safe-looking CoTs may increase the likelihood of safe outputs, causing safe-looking CoTs to be reinforced. We introduce two mitigations to address these two issues, which achieve a Pareto improvement in terms of monitorability and task performance compared to regular training.

papers.title: TRYLOCK: Defense-in-Depth Against LLM Jailbreaks via Layered Preference and Representation Engineering
papers.research_question: How can a defense-in-depth architecture combining weight-level, activation-level, and input-level mechanisms protect LLMs against jailbreak attacks while maintaining usability?
papers.core_contribution: TRYLOCK is a defense-in-depth architecture that combines DPO safety training, RepE activation steering, adaptive sidecar classification, and input canonicalization, achieving an 88.0% relative reduction in Attack Success Rate while reducing over-refusal through adaptive steering.
papers.conclusion: Defense-in-depth with multiple complementary mechanisms (weight modification, activation steering, input classification, and canonicalization) is an effective approach for robust LLM safety against jailbreak attacks, though a trade-off between security and usability remains.
papers.key_findings:
The layered defense reduces Attack Success Rate from 46.5% to 5.6% (88.0% relative reduction) on a 249-prompt attack set.
Each defense layer provides complementary coverage: RepE blocks 36% of attacks that bypass DPO alone, and canonicalization catches 14% of encoding attacks that evade both.
A non-monotonic steering phenomenon was discovered where intermediate steering strength (α=1.0) degrades safety below the DPO-only baseline.
Adaptive steering via a sidecar classifier reduces over-refusal from 60% (fixed α=2.0) to 48% while maintaining identical attack defense.
The defense generalizes to the held-out JailbreakBench, achieving 78.8% relative ASR reduction (52.0% to 11.0%).
papers.limitation:
Evaluation set size and representativeness: the 50-prompt benign set yields wide confidence intervals for over-refusal, and larger diverse evaluations are needed.
Sidecar classifier errors: 18% of attacks are misclassified as SAFE, receiving minimal steering and resulting in higher ASR for those attacks.
future_direction: Extend TRYLOCK to additional base models, non-English languages, and integration with standard LLM serving frameworks.
Improve the sidecar classifier calibration and explore ensemble classifiers for better attack detection.
Conduct larger and more diverse benign evaluations to better characterize usability impact.
papers.abstract: Large language models remain vulnerable to jailbreak attacks, and single-layer defenses often trade security for usability. We present TRYLOCK, the first defense-in-depth architecture that combines four heterogeneous mechanisms across the inference stack: weight-level safety alignment via DPO, activation-level control via Representation Engineering (RepE) steering, adaptive steering strength selected by a lightweight sidecar classifier, and input canonicalization to neutralize encoding-based bypasses. On Mistral-7B-Instruct evaluated against a 249-prompt attack set spanning five attack families, TRYLOCK achieves 88.0% relative ASR reduction (46.5% to 5.6%), with each layer contributing unique coverage: RepE blocks 36% of attacks that bypass DPO alone, while canonicalization catches 14% of encoding attacks that evade both. We discover a non-monotonic steering phenomenon -- intermediate strength (alpha=1.0) degrades safety below baseline -- and provide mechanistic hypotheses explaining RepE-DPO interference. The adaptive sidecar reduces over-refusal from 60% to 48% while maintaining identical attack defense, demonstrating that security and usability need not be mutually exclusive. We release all components -- trained adapters, steering vectors, sidecar classifier, preference pairs, and complete evaluation methodology -- enabling full reproducibility.

papers.title: Eraser: Jailbreaking Defense in Large Language Models via Unlearning Harmful Knowledge
papers.research_question: How can we defend against jailbreaking attacks in Large Language Models by unlearning harmful knowledge while retaining general capabilities and safety alignment?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes Eraser, a jailbreaking defense method that unlearns harmful knowledge via gradient ascent while retaining general knowledge and safety alignment, significantly reducing attack success rates without compromising general capabilities.
papers.conclusion: Eraser effectively defends against jailbreaking by unlearning harmful knowledge, maintaining general performance, and enhancing safety alignment, offering a better balance between harmlessness and usefulness compared to existing methods.
papers.key_findings:
Eraser significantly reduces the Attack Success Rate (ASR) and harmfulness scores for various jailbreaking attacks (AIM, AutoDAN, GCG).
Eraser maintains general capabilities comparable to the base model across multiple benchmarks (e.g., ARC, HellaSwag).
Using random prefixes/suffixes during unlearning (T(·)) enhances defensive capability against jailbreaking.
Unlearning harmful text contributes to defense, but gradient ascent on random token sequences also yields defense at the cost of general performance degradation.
The threshold γ controls the trade-off between defense performance and general capability; a moderate value (e.g., 2) is recommended.
papers.limitation:
Eraser is inefficient as it only defends against specific harmful issues, and enumerating all harmful issues is challenging.
Eraser is only applicable to LLMs that have undergone safety alignment.
future_direction: Future research on jailbreaking defense should focus more on maintaining general capabilities.
More effort is needed to enhance safety alignment so that unlearning methods like Eraser can become an alternative to technologies like RLHF.
papers.abstract: Jailbreaking attacks can enable Large Language Models (LLMs) to bypass the safeguard and generate harmful content. Existing jailbreaking defense methods have failed to address the fundamental issue that harmful knowledge resides within the model, leading to potential jailbreak risks for LLMs. In this paper, we propose a novel defense method called Eraser, which mainly includes three goals: unlearning harmful knowledge, retaining general knowledge, and maintaining safety alignment. The intuition is that if an LLM forgets the specific knowledge required to answer a harmful question, it will no longer have the ability to answer harmful questions. The training of Erase does not actually require the model's own harmful knowledge, and it can benefit from unlearning general answers related to harmful queries, which means it does not need assistance from the red team. The experimental results show that Eraser can significantly reduce the jailbreaking success rate for various attacks without compromising the general capabilities of the model. Our codes are available at https://github.com/ZeroNLP/Eraser.

papers.title: Measuring Chain of Thought Faithfulness by Unlearning Reasoning Steps
papers.research_question: Is the reasoning verbalized in a chain of thought faithful to the model's parametric beliefs?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a framework for measuring parametric faithfulness of generated reasoning (PFF) and an instance called FUR that uses machine unlearning to assess faithfulness of chain-of-thought steps.
papers.conclusion: FUR provides a way to measure parametric faithfulness of CoTs, revealing that CoTs are often faithful but not plausible, indicating a need for specialized alignment.
papers.key_findings:
FUR identifies a larger proportion of faithful CoTs than contextual faithfulness methods like Add-mistake.
Unlearning reasoning steps can change model predictions and also affect the generated CoTs post-unlearning, supporting different answers.
Steps identified as faithful by FUR are not necessarily plausible to humans, highlighting a gap between faithfulness and plausibility.
papers.limitation: FF-HARD does not have perfect recall due to the existence of alternative explanations; a faithful explanation might not affect prediction when unlearned.
future_direction: Improving the specificity evaluation to account for instances that require information from the target step.
Developing better unlearning techniques to verify faithfulness for a larger range of instances.
papers.abstract: When prompted to think step-by-step, language models (LMs) produce a chain of thought (CoT), a sequence of reasoning steps that the model supposedly used to produce its prediction. Despite much work on CoT prompting, it is unclear if reasoning verbalized in a CoT is faithful to the models' parametric beliefs. We introduce a framework for measuring parametric faithfulness of generated reasoning, and propose Faithfulness by Unlearning Reasoning steps (FUR), an instance of this framework. FUR erases information contained in reasoning steps from model parameters, and measures faithfulness as the resulting effect on the model's prediction. Our experiments with four LMs and five multi-hop multi-choice question answering (MCQA) datasets show that FUR is frequently able to precisely change the underlying models' prediction for a given instance by unlearning key steps, indicating when a CoT is parametrically faithful. Further analysis shows that CoTs generated by models post-unlearning support different answers, hinting at a deeper effect of unlearning.

papers.title: LLaVA Steering: Visual Instruction Tuning with 500x Fewer Parameters through Modality Linear Representation-Steering
papers.research_question: How can the number of trainable parameters for visual instruction tuning in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) be significantly reduced by addressing the intrinsic imbalance between text and visual modalities?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Modality Linear Representation-Steering (MoReS), a method that rebalances text and visual modalities in MLLMs by steering visual representations through linear transformations, achieving comparable performance to LoRA with 500x fewer trainable parameters.
papers.conclusion: MoReS provides an efficient and effective approach for visual instruction tuning in MLLMs by addressing modality imbalance, significantly reducing parameter count while maintaining performance, and offering a pathway for more accessible and customizable multimodal model development.
papers.key_findings:
MoReS requires 287 to 1,150 times fewer trainable parameters than LoRA while maintaining competitive performance on multiple visual benchmarks.
MoReS effectively rebalances the attention distribution between visual and textual representations, mitigating the intrinsic modality imbalance in MLLMs.
The method reduces hallucination in MLLMs, as shown by improved performance on POPE and HallucinationBench.
MoReS preserves the LLM's pre-trained world knowledge and performs well on text-only tasks, demonstrating its generalizability.
A dynamic steering ratio mechanism allows MoReS to adapt to tasks of varying complexity, with optimal ratios differing per dataset.
papers.abstract: Jinhe Bi, Yujun Wang, Haokun Chen, Xun Xiao, Artur Hecker, Volker Tresp, Yunpu Ma. Proceedings of the 63rd Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2025.

papers.title: Making Reasoning Matter: Measuring and Improving Faithfulness of Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
papers.research_question: To what degree are the final answers of large language models faithful to their stated chain-of-thought reasoning steps?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces FRODO, a framework to improve the faithfulness of chain-of-thought reasoning in small language models, and uses causal mediation analysis to measure faithfulness.
papers.conclusion: The paper performs a causal mediation analysis showing variation in faithfulness across LLMs and introduces FRODO, which improves faithfulness of chain-of-thought reasoning in small LMs.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs do not reliably use their intermediate reasoning steps when generating an answer.
Instruction-tuned models have a stronger causal effect of reasoning steps on the final answer than RLHF-trained models.
FRODO outperforms strong baselines on four reasoning tasks, improving accuracy by 2-3% over standard fine-tuning.
FRODO improves robustness, showing a 4.5% improvement in controlled indirect effect, and generalizes better to out-of-distribution test sets.
FRODO's rationales are more faithful to its final answer predictions than standard supervised fine-tuning.
papers.limitation:
The causal analysis metric does not evaluate the model's real internal reasoning process.
The method requires additional counterfactual data generated by LLMs, which can be expensive.
Training time increases as training Direct Preference Optimization is a two-step process.
Experiments were run with only 3 random seeds due to complexity.
FRODO is dependent on rationales generated by LLMs, so extra care is needed in production environments.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have been shown to perform better when asked to reason step-by-step before answering a question. However, it is unclear to what degree the model's final answer is faithful to the stated reasoning steps. In this paper, we perform a causal mediation analysis on twelve LLMs to examine how intermediate reasoning steps generated by the LLM influence the final outcome and find that LLMs do not reliably use their intermediate reasoning steps when generating an answer. To address this issue, we introduce FRODO, a framework to tailor small-sized LMs to generate correct reasoning steps and robustly reason over these steps. FRODO consists of an inference module that learns to generate correct reasoning steps using an implicit causal reward function and a reasoning module that learns to faithfully reason over these intermediate inferences using a counterfactual and causal preference objective. Our experiments show that FRODO significantly outperforms four competitive baselines. Furthermore, FRODO improves the robustness and generalization ability of the reasoning LM, yielding higher performance on out-of-distribution test sets. Finally, we find that FRODO's rationales are more faithful to its final answer predictions than standard supervised fine-tuning.

papers.title: Vision-Language Introspection: Mitigating Overconfident Hallucinations in MLLMs via Interpretable Bi-Causal Steering
papers.research_question: How to mitigate overconfident hallucinations in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) by simulating a metacognitive self-correction process that diagnoses and rectifies internal visual-semantic misalignments?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Vision-Language Introspection (VLI), a training-free inference framework that mitigates object hallucinations in MLLMs by first introspectively localizing causal visual anchors and then performing interpretable bi-causal steering to rectify internal representations and calibrate overconfidence.
papers.conclusion: VLI effectively mitigates overconfident hallucinations in MLLMs by introspectively diagnosing visual-semantic conflicts and actively steering internal representations towards verified visual evidence, achieving state-of-the-art performance on standard benchmarks.
papers.key_findings:
VLI reduces the object hallucination rate by 12.67% on MMHal-Bench and improves accuracy by up to 6.33% on POPE compared to baseline models.
Bi-causal steering, which isolates visual evidence from background noise via counterfactual representations, is the most critical component for error rectification.
The method successfully localizes interpretable visual anchors corresponding to high-risk tokens, enabling precise intervention.
VLI demonstrates robust generalization across diverse datasets (MSCOCO, A-OKVQA, GQA) and model architectures (LLaVA-1.5, Qwen3-VL).
Adaptive confidence calibration effectively penalizes ungrounded certainty, mitigating persistent hallucinations driven by blind confidence.
papers.limitation: The method introduces increased computational latency and memory overhead due to the parallel processing of counterfactual branches, though optimization reduces the impact.
papers.abstract: Object hallucination critically undermines the reliability of Multimodal Large Language Models, often stemming from a fundamental failure in cognitive introspection, where models blindly trust linguistic priors over specific visual evidence. Existing mitigations remain limited: contrastive decoding approaches operate superficially without rectifying internal semantic misalignments, while current latent steering methods rely on static vectors that lack instance-specific precision. We introduce Vision-Language Introspection (VLI), a training-free inference framework that simulates a metacognitive self-correction process. VLI first performs Attributive Introspection to diagnose hallucination risks via probabilistic conflict detection and localize the causal visual anchors. It then employs Interpretable Bi-Causal Steering to actively modulate the inference process, dynamically isolating visual evidence from background noise while neutralizing blind confidence through adaptive calibration. VLI achieves state-of-the-art performance on advanced models, reducing object hallucination rates by 12.67% on MMHal-Bench and improving accuracy by 5.8% on POPE.

papers.title: The Blessing and Curse of Dimensionality in Safety Alignment
papers.research_question: What is the role of dimensionality in the linear representation of concepts (like safety) in LLMs, and how can we defend against jailbreaking attacks that exploit these linear structures?
papers.core_contribution: High-dimensional representations in LLMs make them vulnerable to linear jailbreaking attacks; the paper proposes dimensionality reduction methods (FJLT and Bottleneck) to defend against such attacks while preserving safety alignment.
papers.conclusion: High dimensionality is both a blessing (for representing complex concepts) and a curse (for vulnerability to jailbreaking); the proposed dimensionality reduction methods mitigate the curse while preserving alignment.
papers.key_findings:
High-dimensional representations in LLMs lead to linear separability of concepts like safety, which can be exploited for jailbreaking.
Linear probes show that linear separability of concepts emerges in models with sufficiently high hidden dimensions.
The proposed FJLT and Bottleneck methods significantly reduce susceptibility to ActAdd and Ablation jailbreaks.
The Bottleneck method preserves utility on various benchmarks better than FJLT.
Theoretical analysis links the effectiveness of linear jailbreaks to the Rademacher complexity of the linear hypothesis class, which grows with dimension.
papers.limitation:
FJLT model performs poorly on datasets dissimilar to the fine-tuning data.
The methods are primarily effective against linear attacks and may not generalize to non-linear attacks.
The Bottleneck method requires model-specific anchor datasets.
papers.abstract: The focus on safety alignment in large language models (LLMs) has increased significantly due to their widespread adoption across different domains. The scale of LLMs play a contributing role in their success, and the growth in parameter count follows larger hidden dimensions. In this paper, we hypothesize that while the increase in dimensions has been a key advantage, it may lead to emergent problems as well. These problems emerge as the linear structures in the activation space can be exploited, in the form of activation engineering, to circumvent its safety alignment. Through detailed visualizations of linear subspaces associated with different concepts, such as safety, across various model scales, we show that the curse of high-dimensional representations uniquely impacts LLMs. Further substantiating our claim, we demonstrate that projecting the representations of the model onto a lower dimensional subspace can preserve sufficient information for alignment while avoiding those linear structures. Empirical results confirm that such dimensional reduction significantly reduces susceptibility to jailbreaking through representation engineering. Building on our empirical validations, we provide theoretical insights into these linear jailbreaking methods relative to a model's hidden dimensions. Broadly speaking, our work posits that the high dimensions of a model's internal representations can be both a blessing and a curse in safety alignment.

papers.title: Calibrating Reasoning in Language Models with Internal Consistency
papers.research_question: How can internal representations in large language models be used to calibrate reasoning, specifically by measuring inconsistencies between intermediate and final layers during chain-of-thought reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes internal consistency as a novel measure to evaluate LLM confidence in reasoning by examining agreement of latent predictions from intermediate layers, and shows that up-weighting paths with high internal consistency significantly boosts reasoning performance.
papers.conclusion: Internal consistency is a robust indicator of correct reasoning paths and can be leveraged to enhance the reliability of reasoning in LLMs through calibration.
papers.key_findings:
CoT reasoning leads to inconsistencies between middle and final layer representations, indicating uncertainty.
Internal consistency effectively distinguishes between correct and incorrect reasoning paths.
Up-weighting reasoning paths with high internal consistency improves reasoning accuracy across various tasks.
Patterns in attention and feed-forward networks across layers provide insights into the emergence of internal inconsistency.
Layer-weighted aggregation of internal consistency finds transferable patterns that generalize across tasks.
papers.limitation:
The study is restricted to decoder-only models.
The analysis focuses on vanilla chain-of-thought prompting, not other complex prompting techniques.
future_direction: Extending the concept of internal consistency to encoder-decoder models.
Investigating internal consistency under more complex prompting scenarios.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities in various reasoning tasks, aided by techniques like chain-of-thought prompting that elicits verbalized reasoning. However, LLMs often generate text with obvious mistakes and contradictions, raising doubts about their ability to robustly process and utilize generated rationales. In this work, we investigate reasoning in LLMs through the lens of internal representations, focusing on how these representations are influenced by generated rationales. Our preliminary analysis reveals that while generated rationales improve answer accuracy, inconsistencies emerge between the model's internal representations in middle layers and those in final layers, potentially undermining the reliability of their reasoning processes. To address this, we propose internal consistency as a measure of the model's confidence by examining the agreement of latent predictions decoded from intermediate layers. Extensive empirical studies across different models and datasets demonstrate that internal consistency effectively distinguishes between correct and incorrect reasoning paths. Motivated by this, we propose a new approach to calibrate reasoning by up-weighting reasoning paths with high internal consistency, resulting in a significant boost in reasoning performance. Further analysis uncovers distinct patterns in attention and feed-forward modules across layers, providing insights into the emergence of internal inconsistency. In summary, our results demonstrate the potential of using internal representations for self-evaluation of LLMs. Our code is available at github.com/zhxieml/internal-consistency.

papers.title: Reasoning aligns language models to human cognition
papers.research_question: Do language models make decisions under uncertainty like humans do? And if so, what role does chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning play in the underlying decision process?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an active probabilistic reasoning task that disentangles sampling from inference, and a mechanistic model with four latent cognitive variables, showing that chain-of-thought reasoning improves inference quality and shifts LLMs toward human-like decision strategies.
papers.conclusion: Chain-of-thought reasoning shifts language models toward human-like evidence accumulation and belief-to-choice mapping, tightening alignment in inference while leaving a persistent gap in information acquisition.
papers.key_findings:
Extended reasoning (chain-of-thought) is the key determinant of strong performance, driving large gains in inference quality while yielding only modest improvements in active sampling.
Reasoning shifts LLMs toward human-like regimes of evidence accumulation and belief-to-choice mapping, tightening alignment in inference.
LLMs with extended reasoning can match or exceed humans in inference quality but still underperform in sampling quality compared to skilled humans.
A mechanistic model with four interpretable latent variables (Memory, Strategy, Choice Bias, Occlusion Awareness) captures systematic deviations from optimal behavior and places humans and models in a shared cognitive space.
The model fits reveal that chain-of-thought reasoning reduces inference loss and partially aligns sampling strategies, but a gap in information acquisition remains.
papers.abstract: Do language models make decisions under uncertainty like humans do, and what role does chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning play in the underlying decision process? We introduce an active probabilistic reasoning task that cleanly separates sampling (actively acquiring evidence) from inference (integrating evidence toward a decision). Benchmarking humans and a broad set of contemporary large language models against near-optimal reference policies reveals a consistent pattern: extended reasoning is the key determinant of strong performance, driving large gains in inference and producing belief trajectories that become strikingly human-like, while yielding only modest improvements in active sampling. To explain these differences, we fit a mechanistic model that captures systematic deviations from optimal behavior via four interpretable latent variables: memory, strategy, choice bias, and occlusion awareness. This model places humans and models in a shared low-dimensional cognitive space, reproduces behavioral signatures across agents, and shows how chain-of-thought shifts language models toward human-like regimes of evidence accumulation and belief-to-choice mapping, tightening alignment in inference while leaving a persistent gap in information acquisition.

papers.title: On the Impact of Fine-Tuning on Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
papers.research_question: How does fine-tuning affect the accuracy and faithfulness of Chain-of-Thought reasoning in LLMs, and does it compromise general reasoning capabilities?
papers.core_contribution: Fine-tuning LLMs, especially smaller ones, reduces the accuracy and faithfulness of Chain-of-Thought reasoning, with more pronounced negative effects on math tasks.
papers.conclusion: Fine-tuning LLMs, particularly smaller ones, can reduce both the accuracy and faithfulness of Chain-of-Thought reasoning, with more severe effects on math tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Fine-tuning generally reduces CoT reasoning accuracy, with the effect being more pronounced in smaller models.
Fine-tuning can compromise the faithfulness of CoT reasoning, as measured by Early Termination, Paraphrasing, and Filler Substitution tests.
The negative impact on faithfulness is more pronounced when fine-tuning on non-reasoning or common-sense reasoning datasets compared to math reasoning datasets.
For smaller models like Llama-3-8b-Instruct, fine-tuning on non-reasoning datasets leads to larger performance drops on out-of-distribution math tasks.
The rank of QLoRA adapters does not significantly change the overall trends in CoT accuracy and faithfulness degradation.
papers.limitation:
The faithfulness of Chain-of-Thought reasoning has not been extensively studied, and the analysis relies on faithfulness metrics that are still in the early stages of development.
Lack of a deeper investigation into how fine-tuning affects the internal mechanisms of LLMs.
future_direction: Using Inference-Time Intervention (ITI) to analyze how fine-tuning modifies activations of reasoning-related attention heads in LLMs.
Exploring the impact of fine-tuning on newer CoT prompting methods and in-context demonstrations.
papers.abstract: Large language models have emerged as powerful tools for general intelligence, showcasing advanced natural language processing capabilities that find applications across diverse domains. Despite their impressive performance, recent studies have highlighted the potential for significant enhancements in LLMs' task-specific performance through fine-tuning strategies like Reinforcement Learning with Human Feedback (RLHF), supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and Quantized Low-Rank Adapters (Q-LoRA) method. However, previous works have shown that while fine-tuning offers significant performance gains, it also leads to challenges such as catastrophic forgetting and privacy and safety risks. To this end, there has been little to no work in \textit{understanding the impact of fine-tuning on the reasoning capabilities of LLMs}. Our research investigates the effect of fine-tuning on the reasoning abilities of LLMs, addressing critical questions regarding the impact of task-specific fine-tuning on overall reasoning capabilities, the influence of fine-tuning on Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning performance, and the implications for the faithfulness of CoT reasonings. By exploring these dimensions, our study shows the impact of fine-tuning on LLM reasoning capabilities, where the faithfulness of CoT reasoning, on average across four datasets, decreases, highlighting potential shifts in internal mechanisms of the LLMs resulting from fine-tuning processes.

papers.title: Unveiling Confirmation Bias in Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
papers.research_question: How does confirmation bias affect chain-of-thought reasoning behavior in LLMs, and why does its influence vary across questions, reasoning types, and models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that confirmation bias is pervasive in LLMs' chain-of-thought reasoning, affecting both reasoning generation and answer prediction, and explains variance in CoT effectiveness across tasks and models.
papers.conclusion: The study shows that confirmation bias significantly impacts CoT reasoning in LLMs, explaining performance variance across tasks and models, and highlights the difficulty of debiasing strong beliefs.
papers.key_findings:
Internal beliefs (approximated by direct QA probabilities) significantly influence CoT performance at both reasoning generation and answer prediction stages.
Questions with stronger beliefs (lower entropy) are more likely to retain correctness regardless of difficulty, showing confirmation bias.
CoT improvement aligns with the degree to which tasks are prone to confirmation bias, with greater improvement on symbolic reasoning (e.g., math) than on non-symbolic tasks.
Models with weaker beliefs (higher entropy) are more sensitive to the quality and structure of the generated rationale.
Debiasing internal beliefs is challenging, especially when beliefs are strong, as models struggle to follow rationales that contradict their confident prior beliefs.
papers.limitation: The use of entropy as a proxy for belief strength limits analysis to white-box LLMs and multiple-choice questions.
future_direction: Explore confirmation bias using confidence measures applicable to black-box LLMs and open-ended questions.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting has been widely adopted to enhance the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs).However, the effectiveness of CoT reasoning is inconsistent across tasks with different reasoning types.This work presents a novel perspective to understand CoT behavior through the lens of confirmation bias in cognitive psychology.Specifically, we examine how model internal beliefs, approximated by direct questionanswering probabilities, affect both reasoning generation (Q R) and reasoning-guided answer prediction (QR A) in CoT.By decomposing CoT into a two-stage process, we conduct a thorough correlation analysis in model beliefs, rationale attributes, and stage-wise performance.Our results provide strong evidence of confirmation bias in LLMs, such that model beliefs not only skew the reasoning process but also influence how rationales are utilized for answer prediction.Furthermore, the interplay between task vulnerability to confirmation bias and the strength of beliefs also provides explanations for CoT effectiveness across reasoning tasks and models.Overall, this study provides a valuable insight for the needs of better prompting strategies that mitigate confirmation bias to enhance reasoning performance.Code is available at https://github.com/yuewan2/biasedcot.

papers.title: Command-V: Pasting LLM Behaviors via Activation Profiles
papers.research_question: How can behaviors be efficiently transferred from one large language model to another without requiring fine-tuning or backpropagation?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Command-V, a backpropagation-free method that transfers behaviors between LLMs by profiling layer activations, deriving linear converters, and applying donor adapter interventions in the recipient's activation space, matching fine-tuning performance with minimal compute.
papers.conclusion: Command-V provides an efficient, training-free method for behavior transfer across LLMs, pushing the Pareto frontier in cost and performance, with promising future directions for improvement and application.
papers.key_findings:
Command-V matches or exceeds direct fine-tuning performance on safety refusal, jailbreaking, and chain-of-thought reasoning tasks.
The method requires orders of magnitude less compute than fine-tuning and does not need the original training data.
Behaviors can be transferred across different model architectures, though effectiveness varies.
Transfer can sometimes lead to overrefusal or degraded instruction following, especially in smaller models.
Activation profiles built on a general prompt set (LIMA) are effective for transferring task-specific behaviors.
papers.limitation:
Command-V is not useful when the adapters have very little impact on the donor model to begin with.
Model utility can be compromised after applying Command-V, with recipient models sometimes failing to improve task performance or suffering from output collapse.
Architectural divergence between models reduces effectiveness for some behaviors like refusal enhancement and reasoning.
future_direction: Porting behaviors from high-resource to low-resource language models.
Task composition by pasting several specialist adapters into one generalist model.
Exploring non-linear converters or trained converters beyond the least-squares method.
papers.abstract: Retrofitting large language models (LLMs) with new behaviors typically requires full finetuning or distillation-costly steps that must be repeated for every architecture. In this work, we introduce Command-V, a backpropagation-free behavior transfer method that copies an existing residual activation adapter from a donor model and pastes its effect into a recipient model. Command-V profiles layer activations on a small prompt set, derives linear converters between corresponding layers, and applies the donor intervention in the recipient's activation space. This process does not require access to the original training data and needs minimal compute. In three case studies-safety-refusal enhancement, jailbreak facilitation, and automatic chain-of-thought reasoning--Command-V matches or exceeds the performance of direct finetuning while using orders of magnitude less compute. Our code and data are accessible at https://github.com/GithuBarry/Command-V/.

papers.title: SafeSwitch: Steering Unsafe LLM Behavior via Internal Activation Signals
papers.research_question: How can internal activation signals in LLMs be used to predict and dynamically regulate unsafe behavior, balancing safety and utility?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SafeSwitch, a framework that uses a safety prober to monitor internal states and dynamically activate a refusal head to mitigate unsafe outputs, reducing harmful responses by ~80% while preserving utility.
papers.conclusion: SafeSwitch demonstrates LLMs' capacity for self-awareness and reflection regarding safety, offering a promising approach to more nuanced, dynamic, and effective safety controls.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs inherently encode safety-related information (recognition of unsafe instructions and intent to respond) within their internal states.
A two-stage safety prober can predict unsafe behavior with high accuracy (F1 >90%) by decomposing the task into instruction safety and model compliance.
SafeSwitch reduces harmful outputs by approximately 80% on harmful queries (SORRY-Bench, TrustLLM) while maintaining strong utility on benign benchmarks.
SafeSwitch achieves a Pareto optimal balance between safety and utility, outperforming baselines like always-on refusal heads or safety prompts.
The method is parameter-efficient, tuning less than 6% of the original model parameters (prober and refusal head).
papers.limitation: The safety prober can produce false positives (over-refusal) and false negatives (missing unsafe responses), with performance varying across query types and benchmarks.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit exceptional capabilities across various tasks but also pose risks by generating harmful content. Existing safety mechanisms, while improving model safety, often lead to overly cautious behavior and fail to fully leverage LLMs' internal cognitive processes. Inspired by humans' reflective thinking capability, we first show that LLMs can similarly perform internal assessments about safety in their internal states. Building on this insight, we propose SafeSwitch, a dynamic framework that regulates unsafe outputs by utilizing the prober-based internal state monitor that actively detects harmful intentions, and activates a safety head that leads to safer and more conservative responses only when necessary. SafeSwitch reduces harmful outputs by approximately 80% on harmful queries while maintaining strong utility, reaching a Pareto optimal among several methods. Our method is also advantageous over traditional methods in offering more informative, context-aware refusals, and achieves these benefits while only tuning less than 6% of the original parameters. SafeSwitch demonstrates large language models' capacity for self-awareness and reflection regarding safety, offering a promising approach to more nuanced and effective safety controls. Codes for this work are available at https://github.com/Hanpx20/SafeSwitch.

papers.title: Energy-Driven Steering: Reducing False Refusals in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we reduce false refusals (over-refusal) in aligned large language models without compromising safety, using a fine-tuning free, inference-time intervention?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Energy Landscape Steering (ELS), a fine-tuning free framework that uses an externally trained Energy-Based Model to dynamically steer LLM hidden activations during inference, significantly reducing false refusals while maintaining safety and general capabilities.
papers.conclusion: ELS establishes a promising paradigm for building LLMs that simultaneously achieve high safety and low false refusal rates through inference-time activation steering.
papers.key_findings:
ELS raises compliance on the ORB-H false refusal benchmark from 57.3% to 82.6% for Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct while maintaining baseline safety performance.
ELS outperforms existing fine-tuning free methods (Surgical, CAST, AdaSteer, AlphaSteer) in reducing false refusals without degrading safety or general knowledge.
ELS preserves general capabilities (MMLU, ARC-C, MATH accuracy) almost entirely, unlike fine-tuning methods which often degrade them.
ELS shows robustness against multi-turn jailbreak attacks, maintaining lower attack success rates compared to baselines.
The method is computationally efficient, adding minimal overhead during inference compared to other steering techniques.
papers.limitation:
ELS relies on an EBM trained on a fixed dataset, limiting its adaptability to emerging jailbreak tactics unseen during training.
Data labeling operates at the response level, not capturing partial compliance or mid-response refusal patterns, which could be beneficial for reasoning models.
future_direction: Make ELS an online method where the EBM continuously updates based on new interaction data.
Extend data labeling to a more fine-grained, sentence-level annotation scheme to capture partial compliance patterns.
Apply the method to reasoning models with chain-of-thought to rescue misaligned refusals during the thinking period.
papers.abstract: Safety alignment of large language models (LLMs) faces a key challenge: current alignment techniques often only focus on improving safety against harmful prompts, causing LLMs to become over-cautious and refuse to respond to benign prompts. Therefore, a key objective of safe alignment is to enhance safety while simultaneously reducing false refusals. In this paper, we introduce Energy-Driven Steering (EDS), a novel, fine-tuning free framework designed to resolve this challenge through dynamic, inference-time intervention. We trained a lightweight, external Energy-Based Model (EBM) to assign high energy to undesirable (false refusal or jailbreak) states and low energy to desirable (helpful response or safe reject) ones. During inference, EBM maps the LLM's internal activations to an "energy landscape". We use the gradient of the energy function to dynamically steer the LLM's hidden states to low energy regions, correcting the model to generate a desirable response in real-time without modifying its weights. This method decouples behavioral control from the model's core knowledge, offering a flexible solution with minimal computational overhead. Extensive experiments across a wide range of models show our method successfully achieves this objective: it substantially lowers false refusal rates. For example, raising compliance on the ORB-H benchmark from 57.3% to 82.6% while maintaining the baseline safety performance. Our work presents an effective paradigm for building LLMs that achieve both low false refusal rates and high safety.

papers.title: Implicit Chain of Thought Reasoning via Knowledge Distillation
papers.research_question: Can language models reason more effectively using internal hidden states (implicit reasoning) rather than generating explicit chain-of-thought steps?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes implicit chain-of-thought reasoning, which uses internal hidden states for reasoning distilled from a teacher model, enabling faster inference and solving tasks previously not solvable without explicit chain-of-thought.
papers.conclusion: Implicit chain-of-thought reasoning is a promising direction that allows models to reason internally and potentially develop their own reasoning processes, though it currently lags behind explicit CoT in accuracy.
papers.key_findings:
Implicit CoT enables solving multi-digit multiplication tasks that are not solvable with no CoT.
Implicit CoT has higher inference speed than explicit CoT.
The effectiveness of implicit CoT depends on having a sufficient number of layers.
The mixture approach is crucial for tasks with multiple reasoning pathways.
The 'Optimize' step (end-to-end fine-tuning) improves performance.
papers.limitation:
Lack of transparency and interpretability compared to explicit CoT.
Reliance on the teacher's thought process for distillation.
Performance discrepancies compared to explicit CoT.
future_direction: End-to-end joint training using a variational autoencoder by treating internal reasoning as a latent variable.
Using diffusion models to train the thought emulator for multi-modal distributions.
Incorporating implicit CoT into the pretraining process.
papers.abstract: To augment language models with the ability to reason, researchers usually prompt or finetune them to produce chain of thought reasoning steps before producing the final answer. However, although people use natural language to reason effectively, it may be that LMs could reason more effectively with some intermediate computation that is not in natural language. In this work, we explore an alternative reasoning approach: instead of explicitly producing the chain of thought reasoning steps, we use the language model's internal hidden states to perform implicit reasoning. The implicit reasoning steps are distilled from a teacher model trained on explicit chain-of-thought reasoning, and instead of doing reasoning "horizontally" by producing intermediate words one-by-one, we distill it such that the reasoning happens "vertically" among the hidden states in different layers. We conduct experiments on a multi-digit multiplication task and a grade school math problem dataset and find that this approach enables solving tasks previously not solvable without explicit chain-of-thought, at a speed comparable to no chain-of-thought.

papers.title: FaithCoT-Bench: Benchmarking Instance-Level Faithfulness of Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
papers.research_question: do these reasoning steps faithfully represent the model’s internal decision process, or are they merely surface-level accounts designed to appear aligned with the instruction?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces FAITHCOT-BENCH, the first comprehensive benchmark for instance-level Chain-of-Thought faithfulness detection, providing a task formulation, an expert-annotated dataset (FINE-COT), and a systematic evaluation of detection methods.
papers.conclusion: FAITHCOT-BENCH establishes the first comprehensive benchmark for instance-level CoT faithfulness, setting a solid basis for future research toward more interpretable and trustworthy reasoning in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
CoT faithfulness does not align perfectly with task-level accuracy; higher accuracy does not imply more faithful reasoning.
At the instance level, correctness and faithfulness diverge; correct answers can be unfaithful, and incorrect answers can be faithful.
Faithfulness varies systematically across models; larger or more instruction-tuned models produce more faithful CoTs but still have substantial unfaithful rates.
Task type strongly influences faithfulness; knowledge-intensive tasks trigger more unfaithful reasoning than symbolic reasoning tasks.
Problem difficulty and distribution shift increase unfaithfulness.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly rely on Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting to improve problem-solving and provide seemingly transparent explanations. However, growing evidence shows that CoT often fail to faithfully represent the underlying reasoning process, raising concerns about their reliability in high-risk applications. Although prior studies have focused on mechanism-level analyses showing that CoTs can be unfaithful, they leave open the practical challenge of deciding whether a specific trajectory is faithful to the internal reasoning of the model. To address this gap, we introduce FaithCoT-Bench, a unified benchmark for instance-level CoT unfaithfulness detection. Our framework establishes a rigorous task formulation that formulates unfaithfulness detection as a discriminative decision problem, and provides FINE-CoT (Faithfulness instance evaluation for Chain-of-Thought), an expert-annotated collection of over 1,000 trajectories generated by four representative LLMs across four domains, including more than 300 unfaithful instances with fine-grained causes and step-level evidence. We further conduct a systematic evaluation of eleven representative detection methods spanning counterfactual, logit-based, and LLM-as-judge paradigms, deriving empirical insights that clarify the strengths and weaknesses of existing approaches and reveal the increased challenges of detection in knowledge-intensive domains and with more advanced models. To the best of our knowledge, FaithCoT-Bench establishes the first comprehensive benchmark for instance-level CoT faithfulness, setting a solid basis for future research toward more interpretable and trustworthy reasoning in LLMs.

papers.title: Defending Large Language Models Against Jailbreak Attacks via Layer-specific Editing
papers.research_question: How do large language models respond to harmful prompts, and how can we enhance their resilience against jailbreak attacks by editing specific layers?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Layer-specific Editing (LED), a defense method that identifies and edits safety layers in early LLM layers to align them with safe responses, improving jailbreak resistance while maintaining helpfulness.
papers.conclusion: LED effectively defends LLMs against jailbreak attacks by editing specific layers, maintaining helpfulness on benign prompts.
papers.key_findings:
Early safety layers are crucial for defending against harmful prompts; pruning them causes LLMs to generate harmful responses.
Jailbreak attacks do not affect all layers; some layers still decode to refusal tokens.
LED effectively reduces attack success rate across various jailbreak attacks.
LED maintains model helpfulness on benign prompts.
Editing both safety layers and additional middle layers yields the best trade-off between safety and helpfulness.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being adopted in a wide range of real-world applications. Despite their impressive performance, recent studies have shown that LLMs are vulnerable to deliberately crafted adversarial prompts even when aligned via Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback or supervised fine-tuning. While existing defense methods focus on either detecting harmful prompts or reducing the likelihood of harmful responses through various means, defending LLMs against jailbreak attacks based on the inner mechanisms of LLMs remains largely unexplored. In this work, we investigate how LLMs response to harmful prompts and propose a novel defense method termed \textbf{L}ayer-specific \textbf{Ed}iting (LED) to enhance the resilience of LLMs against jailbreak attacks. Through LED, we reveal that several critical \textit{safety layers} exist among the early layers of LLMs. We then show that realigning these safety layers (and some selected additional layers) with the decoded safe response from selected target layers can significantly improve the alignment of LLMs against jailbreak attacks. Extensive experiments across various LLMs (e.g., Llama2, Mistral) show the effectiveness of LED, which effectively defends against jailbreak attacks while maintaining performance on benign prompts. Our code is available at \url{https://github.com/ledllm/ledllm}.

papers.title: Mitigating Safety Tax via Distribution-Grounded Refinement in Large Reasoning Models
papers.research_question: How does distributional gap in safety alignment datasets cause reasoning degradation (safety tax) in large reasoning models, and how can it be mitigated?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes DGR, a data refinement method that aligns safety datasets with the target model's distribution to mitigate safety tax, and shows that distribution shift correlates with reasoning degradation and that safety alignment acts as a knowledge activation mechanism.
papers.conclusion: Distribution shift induced by safety alignment is a primary driver of reasoning degradation in LRMs; DGR mitigates safety tax by aligning safety data with the model's native distribution, and safety alignment functions as a latent-knowledge activator.
papers.key_findings:
DGR effectively mitigates safety tax, improving average reasoning accuracy by +30.2% on DirectRefusal and +21.2% on R1-ACT compared to Vanilla SFT.
The degree of reasoning degradation correlates with the extent of distribution shift, suggesting bridging this gap is central to preserving reasoning capability.
Safety alignment in LRMs may primarily function as a mechanism to activate latent knowledge, as a mere 10 samples are sufficient for activating effective refusal behaviors.
DGR is robust to refinement templates and generalizes to larger model scales (tested on 32B).
Fixed safety templates lead to over-refusal and low lexical diversity, highlighting the need for nuanced safety.
papers.limitation:
Not extending DGR to RL-based safety alignment pipelines.
Limited scaling to massive reasoning models (only tested up to 32B due to computational constraints).
future_direction: Extending DGR to reinforcement learning–based safety alignment pipelines.
More comprehensive evaluations on LRMs with larger parameter scales (e.g., 70B and beyond).
papers.abstract: Safety alignment incurs safety tax that perturbs a large reasoning model's (LRM) general reasoning ability. Existing datasets used for safety alignment for an LRM are usually constructed by distilling safety reasoning traces and answers from an external LRM or human labeler. However, such reasoning traces and answers exhibit a distributional gap with the target LRM that needs alignment, and we conjecture such distributional gap is the culprit leading to significant degradation of reasoning ability of the target LRM. Driven by this hypothesis, we propose a safety alignment dataset construction method, dubbed DGR. DGR transforms and refines an existing out-of-distributional safety reasoning dataset to be aligned with the target's LLM inner distribution. Experimental results demonstrate that i) DGR effectively mitigates the safety tax while maintaining safety performance across all baselines, i.e., achieving \textbf{+30.2\%} on DirectRefusal and \textbf{+21.2\%} on R1-ACT improvement in average reasoning accuracy compared to Vanilla SFT; ii) the degree of reasoning degradation correlates with the extent of distribution shift, suggesting that bridging this gap is central to preserving capabilities. Furthermore, we find that safety alignment in LRMs may primarily function as a mechanism to activate latent knowledge, as a mere \textbf{10} samples are sufficient for activating effective refusal behaviors. These findings not only emphasize the importance of distributional consistency but also provide insights into the activation mechanism of safety in reasoning models.

papers.title: Its Alive: AI Independence Without Human Prompting
papers.research_question: How can representation engineering (RepE) improve transparency and control of AI systems, particularly for safety-relevant concepts?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces representation engineering (RepE) as a top-down approach to AI transparency, providing baselines like Linear Artificial Tomography (LAT) and demonstrating its applicability to reading and controlling safety-relevant concepts in large language models.
papers.conclusion: RepE is a promising top-down approach for enhancing AI transparency and control, with broad applicability to safety-relevant problems, and can accelerate progress in AI safety.
papers.key_findings:
RepE methods can extract representations of high-level concepts like honesty, utility, emotion, and harmfulness.
LAT achieves state-of-the-art on TruthfulQA, improving zero-shot accuracy by 18.1 percentage points.
Representation control can increase model honesty and reduce compliance with harmful instructions, even under jailbreak attempts.
Emotions are represented in LLMs and can be manipulated to affect model compliance and behavior.
RepE provides traction on inner alignment problems like deceptive alignment by enabling monitoring and control of honesty.
future_direction: Further exploration of RepE for transparency and safety of AI systems.
Investigation of emotion representations and their impact on model behavior and concept of self.
Improving robustness and generalization of RepE methods.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we identify and characterize the emerging area of representation engineering (RepE), an approach to enhancing the transparency of AI systems that draws on insights from cognitive neuroscience. RepE places population-level representations, rather than neurons or circuits, at the center of analysis, equipping us with novel methods for monitoring and manipulating high-level cognitive phenomena in deep neural networks (DNNs). We provide baselines and an initial analysis of RepE techniques, showing that they offer simple yet effective solutions for improving our understanding and control of large language models. We showcase how these methods can provide traction on a wide range of safety-relevant problems, including honesty, harmlessness, power-seeking, and more, demonstrating the promise of top-down transparency research. We hope that this work catalyzes further exploration of RepE and fosters advancements in the transparency and safety of AI systems.

papers.title: Causal Front-Door Adjustment for Robust Jailbreak Attacks on LLMs
papers.research_question: How can we robustly jailbreak Large Language Models (LLMs) by modeling the internal safety mechanism as an unobserved confounder and using causal front-door adjustment to sever its confounding effect?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a training-free, causal jailbreaking framework (CFA2) that models safety mechanisms as unobserved confounders, uses Sparse Autoencoders to isolate task intent, and applies weight orthogonalization to physically sever the confounding link, enabling robust and efficient jailbreaking.
papers.conclusion: CFA2 is an effective, efficient, and interpretable framework for jailbreaking LLMs by leveraging causal inference and sparse feature disentanglement to bypass safety guardrails.
papers.key_findings:
CFA2 achieves a state-of-the-art average Attack Success Rate (ASR) of 83.68% across four safety-aligned LLMs, significantly outperforming optimization-based baselines.
The method reduces the complex causal marginalization to a deterministic forward pass with O(1) inference complexity, drastically improving efficiency.
CFA2 maintains high stealthiness by preserving natural language fluency in prompts, as evidenced by low perplexity scores.
Ablation studies confirm the necessity of sparse representations (via SAE) for precise intervention and the superiority of weight orthogonalization over runtime activation clamping.
The method demonstrates robustness across different model architectures and generation lengths.
papers.limitation: The method requires white-box access to the model for SAE training and direct parameter modification, precluding direct application to closed-source models.
future_direction: Distilling the internal causal insights from CFA2 into black-box prompt optimization strategies to bridge the gap to closed-source models.
papers.abstract: Safety alignment mechanisms in Large Language Models (LLMs) often operate as latent internal states, obscuring the model's inherent capabilities. Building on this observation, we model the safety mechanism as an unobserved confounder from a causal perspective. Then, we propose the Causal Front-Door Adjustment Attack (CFA{$^2$}) to jailbreak LLM, which is a framework that leverages Pearl's Front-Door Criterion to sever the confounding associations for robust jailbreaking. Specifically, we employ Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to physically strip defense-related features, isolating the core task intent. We further reduce computationally expensive marginalization to a deterministic intervention with low inference complexity. Experiments demonstrate that CFA{$^2$} achieves state-of-the-art attack success rates while offering a mechanistic interpretation of the jailbreaking process.

papers.title: Jailbreak Attack Initializations as Extractors of Compliance Directions
papers.research_question: How do gradient-based jailbreak attack initializations work, and how can we design an initialization framework that effectively projects prompts along compliance directions to improve attack success rate and reduce computational overhead?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that gradient-based jailbreak attacks and their initializations converge to a single compliance direction, and introduces the CRI framework to project unseen prompts along this direction, improving attack success rates and reducing computational overhead.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that gradient-based jailbreak attacks converge to a single compliance direction and proposes CRI, an initialization framework that projects prompts along this direction, enhancing attack success rates and reducing computational overhead across various attacks, models, and datasets.
papers.key_findings:
Gradient-based jailbreak attacks and self-transfer initializations gradually converge to similar compliance directions.
The Loss at First Step (LFS) metric reliably indicates the number of steps required for a successful attack, enabling selection of effective initializations.
The CRI framework effectively initializes attacks by projecting prompts along compliance directions, increasing Attack Success Rate (ASR) and reducing computational overhead.
CRI performs well across multiple attacks, models, and datasets, highlighting the fragility of safety-aligned LLMs.
The trade-off between the number of initializations (K) and their generalization properties affects performance, with intermediate K (e.g., 5) often optimal.
papers.limitation:
Focus on gradient-based attacks may not generalize to other attack types.
Effectiveness depends on quality and diversity of fine-tuning set.
future_direction: Extending CRI to black-box settings
Integrating CRI with other attack improvements
Applying CRI to other types of attacks and defenses
papers.abstract: Safety-aligned LLMs respond to prompts with either compliance or refusal, each corresponding to distinct directions in the model's activation space. Recent works show that initializing attacks via self-transfer from other prompts significantly enhances their performance. However, the underlying mechanisms of these initializations remain unclear, and attacks utilize arbitrary or hand-picked initializations. This work presents that each gradient-based jailbreak attack and subsequent initialization gradually converge to a single compliance direction that suppresses refusal, thereby enabling an efficient transition from refusal to compliance. Based on this insight, we propose CRI, an initialization framework that aims to project unseen prompts further along compliance directions. We demonstrate our approach on multiple attacks, models, and datasets, achieving an increased attack success rate (ASR) and reduced computational overhead, highlighting the fragility of safety-aligned LLMs. A reference implementation is available at: https://amit1221levi.github.io/CRI-Jailbreak-Init-LLMs-evaluation.

papers.title: Future Events as Backdoor Triggers: Investigating Temporal Vulnerabilities in LLMs
papers.research_question: Can future events serve as backdoor triggers for large language models, and how effective is safety training at removing such backdoors?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that LLMs can distinguish past from future events, and that backdoors triggered by temporal distribution shifts can be trained into models. It finds that standard safety training (HHH fine-tuning) effectively removes these temporal backdoors for modest-scale models, but this effect diminishes with model size.
papers.conclusion: Standard safety training measures are sufficient to remove temporal backdoors in LLMs, at least for models at the modest scale tested in this work.
papers.key_findings:
Linear probes on LLM activations can distinguish past from future news headlines with high accuracy (up to 95% precision).
Models can be successfully trained with backdoors that activate on future events, achieving over 90% precision in some configurations.
Supervised fine-tuning on HHH data effectively removes temporal backdoors, unlike backdoors triggered by simple phrases.
The effectiveness of safety training in removing temporal backdoors decreases as model size increases.
Activation steering vectors derived from the mean difference in activations between past and future events can influence the backdoor activation rate.
papers.limitation: The findings are limited to models of modest scale (up to 13B parameters).
papers.abstract: Backdoors are hidden behaviors that are only triggered once an AI system has been deployed. Bad actors looking to create successful backdoors must design them to avoid activation during training and evaluation. Since data used in these stages often only contains information about events that have already occurred, a component of a simple backdoor trigger could be a model recognizing data that is in the future relative to when it was trained. Through prompting experiments and by probing internal activations, we show that current large language models (LLMs) can distinguish past from future events, with probes on model activations achieving 90% accuracy. We train models with backdoors triggered by a temporal distributional shift; they activate when the model is exposed to news headlines beyond their training cut-off dates. Fine-tuning on helpful, harmless and honest (HHH) data does not work well for removing simpler backdoor triggers but is effective on our backdoored models, although this distinction is smaller for the larger-scale model we tested. We also find that an activation-steering vector representing a model's internal representation of the date influences the rate of backdoor activation. We take these results as initial evidence that, at least for models at the modest scale we test, standard safety measures are enough to remove these backdoors.

papers.title: Iteration Head: A Mechanistic Study of Chain-of-Thought
papers.research_question: How does Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning emerge in transformers, and what are the inner workings and conditions for its appearance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates how CoT reasoning emerges in transformers through the identification and analysis of a specialized attention mechanism called an 'iteration head', which enables efficient iterative reasoning.
papers.conclusion: Transformers can learn to solve iterative tasks efficiently via CoT reasoning by developing inner circuits (iteration heads) dedicated to multistep reasoning, and data curation can guide this process.
papers.key_findings:
Iteration heads, a specific pattern of weights in the first two attention layers, emerge in transformers trained on iterative tasks with CoT.
These heads enable the transformer to solve iterative tasks efficiently by retrieving the current input and previous state to compute the next state.
The iterative reasoning skill granted by iteration heads is transferable between different iterative tasks (e.g., from copying to parity).
Data curation (including easier tasks in training) can guide the model towards learning the iteration head circuit.
Transformers are stateless models, requiring generated states to have a token representation for CoT, which is a limitation for complex iterative algorithms.
papers.limitation: Transformers are stateless models, requiring generated states to have a token representation for CoT, which is a shortcoming for complex iterative algorithms or generic language modeling.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning is known to improve Large Language Models both empirically and in terms of theoretical approximation power. However, our understanding of the inner workings and conditions of apparition of CoT capabilities remains limited. This paper helps fill this gap by demonstrating how CoT reasoning emerges in transformers in a controlled and interpretable setting. In particular, we observe the appearance of a specialized attention mechanism dedicated to iterative reasoning, which we coined "iteration heads". We track both the emergence and the precise working of these iteration heads down to the attention level, and measure the transferability of the CoT skills to which they give rise between tasks.

papers.title: DePass: Unified Feature Attributing by Simple Decomposed Forward Pass
papers.research_question: How can we attribute the behavior of Transformer models to internal computations in a faithful, fine-grained, and unified way without requiring auxiliary training?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces DePass, a unified framework for feature attribution in Transformers based on a single decomposed forward pass that freezes attention scores and MLP activations, enabling lossless, additive decomposition and faithful attribution without auxiliary training.
papers.conclusion: DePass is a simple and efficient framework for interpreting Transformer models via a decomposed forward pass, achieving faithful attribution across token-level, component-level, and subspace-level granularities and serving as a general-purpose tool for mechanistic interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
DePass enables lossless additive decomposition of hidden states throughout the forward pass of Transformer models.
DePass provides more faithful token-level attribution compared to gradient-based and attention-based baseline methods.
DePass can attribute model behavior to specific architectural components (attention heads, MLP neurons) and to arbitrary linear subspaces.
DePass can be combined with Sparse Autoencoders (SAE) for token-level attribution of interpretable features.
DePass is computationally efficient, requiring only a single forward pass and significantly faster than exhaustive ablation methods.
papers.limitation:
DePass only captures information flow through the output-value (OV) circuit and does not explain query-key (QK) circuit interactions.
Decomposing the QK circuit would involve quadratic complexity and remains a challenging open problem.
Practical memory constraints require grouping components for fine-grained analysis, which can increase time costs.
future_direction: Unwrapping the QK circuit to understand its interactions is a key direction for future work.
Releasing a general-purpose toolkit supporting a broad range of Transformer models.
Optimizing computational efficiency and improving hardware deployment strategies to support higher-resolution attribution.
papers.abstract: Attributing the behavior of Transformer models to internal computations is a central challenge in mechanistic interpretability. We introduce DePass, a unified framework for feature attribution based on a single decomposed forward pass. DePass decomposes hidden states into customized additive components, then propagates them with attention scores and MLP's activations fixed. It achieves faithful, fine-grained attribution without requiring auxiliary training. We validate DePass across token-level, model component-level, and subspace-level attribution tasks, demonstrating its effectiveness and fidelity. Our experiments highlight its potential to attribute information flow between arbitrary components of a Transformer model. We hope DePass serves as a foundational tool for broader applications in interpretability.

papers.title: Pruning for Protection: Increasing Jailbreak Resistance in Aligned LLMs Without Fine-Tuning
papers.research_question: How does model compression, specifically pruning, affect the jailbreak resistance of aligned large language models?
papers.core_contribution: Moderate pruning using WANDA increases jailbreak resistance in aligned LLMs without fine-tuning, while preserving performance on standard benchmarks.
papers.conclusion: Moderate pruning can improve jailbreak resistance in safety-trained LLMs, but excessive pruning reduces safety, suggesting that careful pruning can aid in deploying safe models.
papers.key_findings:
Pruning at 10-30% sparsity improves jailbreak resistance, with peak improvement at 20% sparsity for LLaMA-2 Chat.
The degree of safety improvement correlates with the initial model's safety level; models with more safety training show greater improvement.
Pruned models exhibit sharper attention patterns and are less distracted by jailbreak pretexts.
Pruned models assign higher perplexity to jailbreak constructs, indicating increased sensitivity to out-of-distribution prompts.
Pruning enhances resistance against both manual jailbreak attempts and automated attacks like GCG.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to 7-billion parameter models and WANDA pruning; results may not generalize to larger models or other compression techniques.
future_direction: Extend analysis to larger models
Explore other compression techniques beyond WANDA pruning
papers.abstract: This paper investigates the impact of model compression on the way Large Language Models (LLMs) process prompts, particularly concerning jailbreak resistance. We show that moderate WANDA pruning can enhance resistance to jailbreaking attacks without fine-tuning, while maintaining performance on standard benchmarks.
